title: How To Be A Classroom Management Pro
author: Michael Linsin
summary: In this partly promotional but reflective piece, Michael Linsin describes the origin of Smart Classroom Management as a response to conflicting and misleading advice circulating among teachers, and explains how he distilled hundreds of individually effective SCM strategies down into a smaller set of core, philosophically aligned strategies. He credits a particularly challenging class he was given as the catalyst for this synthesis, explaining that applying these core strategies to his own difficult group led to a genuine transformation from a chaotic to a respectful classroom. The article announces the resulting online course, The Total Classroom Management Makeover, as a structured pathway for teachers to move from struggling with management to developing it as a reliable, repeatable skill. While it functions as a course announcement, it includes substantive reflection on why so many teachers struggle with management despite good intentions — largely due to combining incompatible philosophies from different sources.
points: Many teachers struggle with classroom management not from lack of effort but from combining strategies drawn from philosophically incompatible sources.
SCM's approach is built on the premise that its strategies are meant to be used together, philosophically aligned, and to compound in effectiveness over time.
Hundreds of individually effective strategies were eventually distilled down into a smaller number of core strategies that produce a naturally effective overall skill set.
The author credits successfully transforming one of his most challenging classes as the real-world proof of concept behind the resulting course.
The core strategies are described as simple dos and don'ts, not clever psychological tricks, that require consistent, uncompromising application to work.
quotes: A few years ago, I wrote an article called 50 Things You Don't Have To Do For Effective Classroom Management. It resonated with a lot of readers.
Furthermore, many teachers are using methods from opposing philosophies that have no business in the same classroom together. The result is more misbehavior, not less.
All of our strategies—from how to build relationships to how to hold students accountable—are philosophically aligned. They’re meant to be used together and get stronger over time.

Eventually, I realized that all SCM strategies, although individually effective, fall under the umbrella of a relatively small number of key strategies—or core strategies—that empower the teacher-user with a naturally effective skill set.
It is this same group of core strategies that I relied on to transform my difficult class into the respectful one that I looked forward to being with every day.
They aren’t fancy, colorful, or complex and they don’t involve any clever psychological manipulation or trickery.
